messages:
maria: quick architecture question — for Private deployments are we leaning toward a thin control-plane mesh (single relay fabric for all customers) or fully isolated per-customer endpoints? thinking about peering counts, upgrades, and audit boundaries :thinking:

jordan: short answer: tradeoffs. thin mesh => far fewer peering links and simpler routing rules, but higher blast radius + more careful auth separation needed. per-customer endpoints => stronger isolation, more HW/network ops.

sam: i like a hybrid: isolate control plane per customer (separate mTLS identities, audit trails) but allow a shared, regional relay layer for data-plane egress to reduce peering complexity. control plane handles model/versioning only, relay handles streaming tokens.

maria: yeah that mirrors my thought. curious about practical limits: route table size, TGW costs, and cross-account peering mgmt. anyone measured route propagation limits in practice?

jordan: AWS RT rules ~50-100 routes per table depending on config. at scale per-customer routes get painful. we should prefer Transit Gateway or use proxy relays with NAT to reduce per-customer route entries. TGW has cost but centralizes.

ashley: one important operational angle: upgrades. if control plane is thin & shared, a mis-deploy can impact many tenants. can we do canary per-customer if control plane shared? not without isolation knobs.

sam: canary strategy: run control-plane-microservices with tenant-scoped feature flags + canary routing. but that requires robust feature flagging and rollout policies. complexity vs per-tenant deploys.

ashley: also ip addressing. if we put relays in a regional VPC, we need a stable CIDR scheme. suggestion: allocate per-tenant overlay prefixes (e.g., /28 or /26) mapped to relay instances to avoid route explosion on customer side.

maria: example config snippet for a relay NAT approach — this is what i sketched in spike: 
```
# relay route table (regional)
Destination: 10.200.0.0/16 -> local relay subnet
Customer CIDR -> nat-gateway or ENI associated with customer prefix
# on customer side: single static route -> relay TGW attachment
```

jordan: nice. another option: use per-customer proxy endpoints (ALB/NLB) in the customer account with private link to us. trades peering for endpoint management. pro: strong isolation and AWS-managed scaling. con: many endpoints to track and extra costs per endpoint.

sam: +1 on PrivateLink for high-security customers. For PLG/default customers, relay fabric + TGW seems cheaper. we should probably tier: PrivateLink for enterprise, relay mesh for self-serve.

maria: how about observability and attribution? shared relay must propagate tenant id in traces and request headers and have per-tenant metrics. any suggestions on low-overhead tagging?

ashley: require signed tenant metadata in TLS handshake (mTLS SNI or x-tenant header signed by client cert) so relays can't be tricked. then enrich traces with that identity at ingress. add sampling rules per-tenant.

infra-bot: deploy-bot: perf tests from spike-2026-03 show relay hop adds median +1.6ms and 99p +6ms under 50MB streaming sessions. CPU cost on relay ~0.08 vCPU per 100 concurrent streams.

maria: that perf number is acceptable for most users. for ultra-low-latency customers (>10ms SLO) we should recommend private endpoints in-region.

jordan: we also need a clear failover story: if relay region is degraded, fallback to customer-managed endpoint or cross-region relay. policy should be per-tenant togglable.

sam: and RBAC: ensure control-plane admin actions (rollout, revoke keys) are logged per-tenant. even if control plane is shared, cryptographic separation of keys + auditable events is non-negotiable.

maria: ok actionable summary: 1) propose hybrid default: per-tenant control-plane isolation logical (separate identities, audit), shared regional relay fabric for data-plane. 2) tiering: PrivateLink for enterprise/high-SLA, relay for self-serve. 3) use TGW or proxying to avoid route-table explosion. 4) must implement tenant identity propagation and per-tenant metrics. 5) document failover and canary patterns.

ashley: agree. i'll draft a short RFC addendum with architecture diagrams and operational runbooks (upgrade/canary + incident playbook). tagging @maria @jordan for review. :thumbsup:

maria: great, thanks. please include cost model estimate for TGW vs PrivateLink in the doc.

jordan: will add a sketch for CIDR allocation and examples of `ip route` config for partners.

sam: i'll add tests for relay perf and a simple PoC for mTLS tenant assertions.

infra-bot: reminder: next infra sync on Tue will review the RFC addendum. :calendar:
